title: Picot
subtitle: Three chains closed into a loop — the decorative edging point
excerpt: A picot is three chains closed with a slip stitch back into the first chain, forming a tiny pointed loop. Picots decorate the tops of lace edgings, the tips of shawl points, and the edge of baby garments. The same three-chain structure applies to both standard and double picots.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), lace and edging chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 1. Picot edging as a traditional Victorian crochet finish.
heroPrompt: A lace edging strip showing a row of picot loops along the top, cream cotton thread, three-chain picots pointing upward, natural background.

glossaryTerms.definition: Three chains closed back into the first chain with a slip stitch, forming a small decorative pointed loop. Used to finish lace edgings, shawl tips, and baby garment edges. Abbreviated p.

content.text: is simply ch 3, sl st back into the first chain of those three. That closes the three chains into a tiny triangle pointing upward. It takes three seconds to work and is the standard finish for any edging that needs a decorative serrated edge rather than a plain row.
Work to the stitch where the picot should sit. Chain 3.
Insert the hook back into the FIRST chain of those three (the chain closest to the work, furthest from the hook).
Yarn over and pull through both the chain and the loop on the hook. One loop remains. The picot is closed.
Continue the edging pattern, working the next stitch into the same or following stitch as the pattern directs.
On a finished piece with a straight edge, work the picot edging as follows:
Join yarn to one corner of the edge. Ch 1.
*Dc in next 2 stitches (or 3, depending on yarn weight), picot (ch 3, sl st into first ch), dc in same place; repeat from * evenly across the edge.
Fasten off and sew in the ends.

attrs.title: 4-chain picot for a larger point
attrs.body: A 4-chain picot (ch 4, sl st back into first chain) gives a taller, more visible point. Use it on chunky yarn or on decorative shawl edgings where the smaller 3-chain picot would be lost.

items.symptom: The picot does not form a clean triangle — it flops to one side
items.cause: The slip stitch re-insert went into the second or third chain rather than the first.
items.fix: After chaining 3, count back to the chain immediately against the working stitch. The first chain is the one at the base of the three, attached to the last dc or stitch worked. The slip stitch goes into that one.

items.symptom: The picots are uneven heights along the edge
items.cause: Inconsistent tension on the three chains.
items.fix: Work all three chains to the same length. Hold the last chain's loop firmly before sliding to the next one.

content.text: A picot lace edging uses picots between dc groups across a foundation row, with more picots added on return rows — this is the Dillmont-style lace edging that finishes Victorian household linens. Try working a 10-stitch sample: dc in 3 sts, picot, dc in 3 sts, picot, and repeat — this gives you the rhythm of picot placement.
